abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Tinengotinib is a spectrum-selective multi-kinase inhibitor targeting FGFR1–3, JAK1/2, VEGFRs, and Aurora A/B kinases. This phase Ib/II clinical trial (NCT05253053) evaluated tinengotinib as monotherapy (Arm A, n = 53, in Chinese patients with advanced solid tumors) and in combination with atezolizumab (Arm B, n = 31, in patients with advanced biliary tract cancer). Each arm comprised a dose-escalation phase with standard 3 + 3 design (phase Ib) followed by a dose-expansion phase (phase II). The primary endpoints of the phase Ib were safety, tolerability, dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and dose selection for expansion, with secondary endpoints of efficacy (phase II) and pharmacokinetics. The trial met pre-specified primary endpoints: tinengotinib was well tolerated without DLTs, and MTD was not reached. Tinengotinib demonstrated antitumor activity both as monotherapy (objective response rate [ORR]: 16.7% in Arm A) and combined with atezolizumab (ORR: 22.6% in Arm B). In predefined exploratory subgroup analysis, notable efficacy was observed in cholangiocarcinoma (ORR: 30.8% in Arm A [n = 13]; 25.0% in Arm B [n = 28]). Tinengotinib monotherapy achieved favorable response in cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2 fusion progressing on prior FGFR inhibitor (ORR: 66.7%). In patients with cholangiocarcinoma previously treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (n = 20), the combination regimen achieved an ORR of 20.0% and a disease control rate of 75.0%. These findings support further development of tinengotinib, both as monotherapy and in combination with immunotherapy.

sec.p: Subject terms: Cancer, Cancer therapy

abstract.p: Tinengotinib is a spectrum-selective multi-kinase inhibitor targeting several oncogenic and immunoregulatory pathways, including FGFR1–3, JAK1/2, VEGFRs, and Aurora A/B kinases. Here the authors report the results of a phase Ib/II trial of tinengotinib as monotherapy or combined with anti-PDL1 atezolizumab in patients with advanced solid tumors.

sec.p: Received 2025 Nov 17; Accepted 2026 Apr 20; Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) genetic alterations, particularly FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements, have emerged as key oncogenic drivers in various solid tumors, including cholangiocarcinoma1. However, tumor heterogeneity and acquired resistance limit the response to single-target therapies2–4. Beyond FGFR signaling, additional pathways such as Aurora kinase A/B, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR), and Janus kinase (JAK) have been implicated in regulating both tumor cell-intrinsic features and the microenvironment5–7. These interconnected oncogenic circuits suggest that a multi-targeted strategy may offer a promising approach to overcoming resistance in molecularly defined patient subsets.

Tinengotinib (TT-00420) is a spectrum-selective, orally bioavailable multi-kinase inhibitor targeting key oncogenic and immunoregulatory signaling pathways, including FGFR1-3, JAK1/2, VEGFRs, and Aurora kinases A and B8. In early phase studies, tinengotinib monotherapy has shown clinical activity in heavily pretreated patients with advanced cancers, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma8. Across these studies, tinengotinib exhibited manageable toxicity and a favorable pharmacokinetic (PK) profile compatible with once-daily dosing9,10. Importantly, tinengotinib led to notable responses and durable disease control in patients with FGFR2 fusion-positive cholangiocarcinoma, including those with progression after prior FGFR inhibitor therapies (ORR: 37.5%), for whom no effective treatment options currently exist11.

Despite recent advances with FGFR-targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), their combination has not been thoroughly investigated. Emerging evidence suggests that combining targeted therapy with immunotherapy may enhance efficacy through complementary mechanisms12. Preclinical study13 of tinengotinib has shown that it not only disrupts tumor cell signaling, but also promotes vascular normalization and enhances T-cell–mediated antitumor immunity when combined with PD-1 inhibitors. These findings support the evaluation of combining tinengotinib with ICIs as a strategy to potentiate therapeutic benefit in advanced solid tumors, particularly in immunologically “cold” tumors such as cholangiocarcinoma14.

Here, we show the results of a phase Ib/II trial evaluating tinengotinib, both as monotherapy and in combination with atezolizumab, in patients with advanced solid tumors. Tinengotinib shows a manageable safety profile and promising antitumor activity, with notable efficacy in cholangiocarcinoma—particularly in patients with FGFR2 fusions who have progressed on prior FGFR inhibitors and in those previously treated with ICIs. These findings support the continued clinical development of tinengotinib as monotherapy and in combination with immunotherapy.

sec.title: Patient disposition and baseline characteristics
sec.p: From March 2022 to August 2024, 84 patients were enrolled and treated, comprising 53 patients in Arm A and 31 patients in Arm B. A detailed summary of subject disposition is presented in Fig. 1. Baseline characteristics of the enrolled participants are summarized in Table 1. In both arms, males constituted the more prevalent sex (Arm A: 62.3%, Arm B: 67.7%). In Arm A, the most common tumor types were prostate cancer (37.7%) and cholangiocarcinoma (26.4%). In Arm B, most patients (90.3%) had cholangiocarcinoma, and a small subset had gallbladder cancer (9.7%). Most patients were heavily treated, with ≥2 prior lines of therapy in 83.0% of Arm A and 58.1% of Arm B. As shown in Table 2, patients with prior exposure to chemotherapy was 90.6% and 96.8%, while prior immunotherapy was 34.0% and 71.0% in Arm A and Arm B, respectively. Of the 14 patients with cholangiocarcinoma in Arm A, FGFR alterations were observed in half of them (n = 7), with five cases of FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement and two cases of FGFR3 fusion/rearrangement. Most patients in Arm B had FGFR wild-type cholangiocarcinoma (n = 26, 83.9%). Notably, four (7.5%) patients in Arm A and one (3.2%) in Arm B had experienced disease progression following prior FGFR inhibitor therapy.

sec.title: Safety, tolerability and maximum tolerated dose (MTD)
sec.p: The exposure duration and relative dose intensity of tinengotinib and atezolizumab are summarized in Tables S1 and S2. No dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) were reported in the phase Ⅰb dose-escalation parts of Arm A and Arm B. The MTDs of tinengotinib monotherapy or combination with atezolizumab were not reached. Tinengotinib 10 mg QD monotherapy, tinengotinib 8 mg and 10 mg QD combined with atezolizumab 1200 mg intravenous infusion every 21 days were selected as the expansion doses in phase II for Arm A and Arm B, respectively.

In Arm A, the incidence of grade ≥3 TEAEs was 66.7% at both 8 mg and 10 mg QD of tinengotinib, and 100.0% at 12 mg QD during phase Ⅰb. Tinengotinib showed more favorable safety and tolerability profiles under the 10 mg QD dose and below (Supplementary Table 3). The incidence of grade ≥3 TEAEs was 86.4% in phase II, with tinengotinib-related grade ≥3 TEAEs reported in 70.5% of patients. For the total patients in Arm A, discontinuation due to TEAEs occurred in 5.7% (tinengotinib-related: 3.8%) of all patients. In Arm A, the most frequent tinengotinib-related grade ≥3 TEAEs were hypertension (24.5%) (Table 3).

caption.p: Common grade ≥3 treatment-related TEAEs in Arms A and B (≥5% incidence, safety analysis set)

sec.p: In Arm B, the incidence of grade ≥3 TEAEs was 100.0%, 66.7% and 100.0% at 8 mg, 10 mg, and 12 mg QD of tinengotinib combined with atezolizumab during phase Ⅰb (Supplementary Table 3). Of these, 66.7%, 66.7%, and 100.0% were considered related to tinengotinib. TEAEs led to tinengotinib discontinuation in one patient (3.2%) which were not related to treatment (Supplementary Table 3). In Arm B, commonly observed grade ≥3 combination treatment-related TEAEs was also hypertension (22.6%) (Table 3).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: The efficacy outcomes based on the EAS are summarized in Supplementary Table 4. In Arm A (EAS, n = 42), assessed by RECIST 1.1, one patient (2.4%) achieved a CR and six (14.3%) achieved a PR, resulting in an ORR of 16.7% (95% CI: 7.0-31.4). Twenty-six patients (61.9%) experienced SD, contributing to a DCR of 78.6% (95% CI: 63.2-89.7). The median DoR was 8.5 months (95% CI: 5.7-not available [NA]), and the median PFS was 5.2 months (95% CI: 3.5-6.9). Based on the FAS, the 1-year OS rate was 34.4% (95% CI: 21.6-47.5) in Arm A (n = 53). The efficacy outcomes across different dose groups are shown in Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Fig. 1, with the expanded dose of tinengotinib at 10 mg QD showing an ORR of 15.2% (95% CI: 5.1-31.9) and notable tumor reduction (Supplementary Fig. 1).

In Arm B (EAS, n = 31), the ORR and DCR among patients with BTC (n = 31) were 22.6% (95% CI: 9.6–41.1) and 71.0% (95% CI: 52.0–85.8), respectively, with a median PFS of 4.1 months (95% CI: 2.3–11.0, Supplementary Fig. 2) by both RECIST 1.1 and iRECIST. Based on FAS, the 1-year OS rate was 61.8% (95% CI: 41.3–76.9) in Arm B (n = 31). The efficacy outcomes across different dose groups in phase II suggested ORRs of 20.0% (95% CI: 2.5–55.6) and 16.7% (95% CI: 2.1–48.4) with the expanded doses of tinengotinib at 8 mg and 10 mg QD combined with atezolizumab, respectively, either using RECIST 1.1 (Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 2) or iRECIST (Supplementary Table 7). The ORRs were 23.1% (95% CI: 5.0–53.8) and 20% (95% CI: 4.3–48.1) at doses of tinengotinib at 8 mg and 10 mg QD combined with atezolizumab in the combined population from phase Ib and II, respectively.

Efficacy outcomes were further evaluated in specific types of tumors (Table 4, Figs. 2 and 3). In Arm A, patients with cholangiocarcinoma (n = 13) achieved notable outcomes, with an ORR of 30.8% (95% CI: 9.1–61.4), a DCR of 76.9% (95% CI: 46.2–95.0), and a median PFS of 7.0 months (95% CI: 1.3–11.4, Fig. 3a). Among the seven patients with FGFR-altered cholangiocarcinoma, three achieved PR and three had SD, resulting in an ORR of 42.9% (95% CI: 9.9–81.6) and a DCR of 85.7% (95% CI: 42.1–99.6) (Fig. 2a). Notably, in the subset of cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement and prior FGFR inhibitor treatment (n = 3), two patients achieved PR and one had SD, yielding an ORR of 66.7% (95%CI: 9.4–99.2) and a DCR of 100.0% (95% CI: 29.2–100.0) (Fig. 2a). Similarly, in Arm B, the ORR and DCR among patients with cholangiocarcinoma (n = 28) were 25.0% (95% CI: 10.7–44.9) and 75.0% (95% CI: 55.1–89.3), respectively, with a median PFS of 5.7 months (95% CI: 2.4–15.3, Fig. 3b). The combination regimen also showed preliminary efficacy for patients who failed from previous ICIs. There were 20 patients with cholangiocarcinoma who had previously received ICIs, and four of them achieved PR in this study, corresponding to an ORR of 20.0% (95% CI: 5.7–43.7) and a DCR of 75.0% (95% CI: 50.9–91.3) (Fig. 2b). Additionally, two of them who had FGFR2-altered cholangiocarcinoma both achieved SD.

sec.p: As for prostate cancer in Arm A (n=11), one patient with prostate cancer, with the absence of measurable target lesions at baseline, achieved CR, demonstrated by the disappearance of all non-target lesions. Nine patients achieved SD, resulting in an ORR of 9.1% (95% CI: 0.23-41.3) and DCR of 90.9% (95% CI: 58.7–99.8) for prostate cancer (Supplementary Table 4). Among 11 patients with FGFR-altered advanced solid tumors other than cholangiocarcinoma in Arm A, an ORR of 18.2% (95% CI: 2.3–51.8) and a DCR of 81.8% (95% CI: 48.2–97.7) were observed, with two of them who had prior FGFR inhibitor exposure both achieving SD (Fig. 2a).

The efficacy outcomes of Arm A and Arm B are not directly comparable due to distinct disease characteristics between the arms. Particularly, Arm A predominantly enrolled patients with FGFR alterations, whereas Arm B consisted mostly of those with FGFR wild-type. Given that FGFR status, rather than prior exposure to immunotherapy, is a critical factor influencing the efficacy of tinengotinib monotherapy, we further performed predefined exploratory subgroup analysis for cholangiocarcinoma stratified by molecular characteristics and prior treatments in Arm A and Arm B (Supplementary Table 8, Fig. 4). For instance, in patients with FGFR2 wild-type cholangiocarcinoma, the ORR was 12.5% (95% CI, 0.3-52.7) in Arm A and 26.9% (95% CI, 11.6-47.8) in Arm B, suggesting a potential numerical improvement with the addition of atezolizumab in certain clinically relevant subgroup.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: PK parameters are summarized in Supplementary Table 9, with corresponding plasma concentration-time profiles presented in Supplementary Fig. 3. Across all dose groups, the median time to maximum plasma concentration (Tmax) ranged from 1 to 6 hours. The geometric mean terminal elimination half-life (t½) ranged from 22.6 to 64.2 hours. Following repeated dosing, geometric mean accumulation ratios for maximum plasma concentration (Rac Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 hours (Rac AUC₀-₂₄) ranged from 1.5 to 2.6 and from 1.7 to 3.6, respectively. Steady-state concentrations were achieved by Day 15 across all dose levels of both arms. No significant linear dose-exposure relationship was identified. The levels of maximum plasma concentration and area under the plasma concentration-time curve at each dose level were comparable between Arm A and Arm B.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This phase Ⅰb/II study demonstrated that tinengotinib, either as monotherapy or in combination with atezolizumab, was well tolerated with promising antitumor activity in patients with advanced solid tumors, particularly cholangiocarcinoma. The safety profile was manageable, with no unexpected AEs. PK parameters supported QD dosing, and the RP2D was established as 10 mg. Tinengotinib demonstrated meaningful clinical benefit in patients with FGFR alterations, including those who had previously failed FGFR-targeted therapies, suggesting its potential in the post-FGFR inhibitor setting. Furthermore, activity was also observed in FGFR-altered tumors in FGFR inhibitor-naïve patients, supporting further investigation of tinengotinib in earlier lines of therapy. The combination of tinengotinib and atezolizumab showed the potential to optimize immunotherapy strategies and broaden treatment options.

Emerging clinical evidence supports the antitumor activity of tinengotinib across multiple solid tumors, particularly cholangiocarcinoma. In the first-in-human phase I study, tinengotinib demonstrated a favorable safety profile and preliminary efficacy in a pan-solid tumor population, predominantly of Western ancestry, with early signals of activity in FGFR-altered cholangiocarcinoma and other tumor types8. More recently, Javle et al. reported a multicenter phase II trial showing clinically meaningful activity of tinengotinib monotherapy in advanced cholangiocarcinoma, particularly in patients with FGFR2 fusions who had progressed on prior FGFR inhibitors15. The present phase Ib/II study extends the clinical evidence for tinengotinib in several important aspects. Our results validate prior efficacy signals in a Chinese population, supporting consistency across distinct ethnic and genetic backgrounds. By focusing on predefined arms, particularly cholangiocarcinoma, this study further strengthens evidence for tinengotinib activity in patients who have failed prior FGFR-targeted therapies. Importantly, Arm B prospectively explores the combination of tinengotinib with ICI, including in patients with prior ICI exposure. Together, these studies support continued development of tinengotinib while underscoring the need for future randomized trials to define its optimal clinical positioning.

Tinengotinib monotherapy demonstrated encouraging activity in patients with FGFR2 fusion/rearranged cholangiocarcinoma who had previously progressed on FGFR-targeted therapies. In three patients who had failed prior FGFR inhibitors, the ORR was 66.7% and the DCR was 100%. Furthermore, the patients in Arm A were generally heavily pretreated. In contrast, most existing and investigational FGFR inhibitors have been evaluated primarily in FGFR inhibitor-naïve or less pretreated populations4,16–18. The treatment options remain limited for patients who have progressed after FGFR inhibitors, and the results of this study suggest that tinengotinib is a highly promising therapeutic option for this treatment-refractory population.

Key mechanisms of resistance to FGFR inhibitors, such as futibatinib, involve FGFR kinase domain mutations and pose therapeutic challenges in cholangiocarcinoma19,20. As a spectrum-selective small-molecule kinase inhibitor, tinengotinib has high-affinity binding to the active FGFR2 kinase domain, mediated by three hydrogen bonds in the hinge region—compared to one or two in earlier inhibitors—resulting in a much stronger affinity for FGFR221. Tinengotinib has shown activity against multiple FGFR kinase domain mutations and variants such as N550K and V565F21. Tinengotinib can lead to diminished variant allele frequencies of driver mutations and FGFR2 alterations, including N550D, V565I, and M538I. These suggest tinengotinib as a rational and promising therapeutic for overcoming resistance to FGFR inhibitors.

ICIs have emerged as an important therapeutic strategy in the treatment of advanced BTC22,23. However, therapeutic options for patients who progress after ICI-based treatment remain limited, given ICI rechallenge is seldom effective. Several targets (such as FGFRs and Aurora A) of tinengotinib may work synergistically with ICIs. FGFR inhibition was shown to abrogate anti-PD-1-induced expansion of Tregs, thereby alleviating immunosuppression24. The combination of FGFR inhibition with ICI also significantly enhanced CD8 + T cell infiltration, T cell activation, and effector function24. Inhibition of Aurora A can deplete tumor-promoting myeloid cells and enrich anti-cancer T lymphocytes, thereby enhancing the efficacy of ICI25. Additionally, inhibition of Aurora A can upregulate the expression of PD-L1 and B7-H3, which may also sensitize tumors to ICI treatment26. These mechanisms may collectively contribute to improved ICI response when combined with tinengotinib. In this context, our preclinical findings also demonstrated that the combination of a PD-1 antibody with tinengotinib significantly suppressed tumor growth in murine models, with superior antitumor activity compared to either agent alone. These results suggest that tinengotinib may potentiate the effects of PD-1 blockade. In this study, tinengotinib combined with atezolizumab achieved an ORR of 20.0% and a DCR of 75.0% in patients with cholangiocarcinoma and previously treated with ICIs, regardless of the FGFR gene status. These results compare favorably with previous attempts to combine targeted therapies with ICIs in BTC, with ORRs ranging from 3.3% to 13.8%27–29. Moreover, the previous combinations of other FGFR inhibitors with immunotherapy are mostly investigated in other tumor types30,31, while data specific to cholangiocarcinoma remain sparse. The Arm B in this study provides valuable clinical evidence supporting the efficacy of an FGFR-targeted agent in combination with immunotherapy in ICI-pretreated cholangiocarcinoma.

However, these findings should be interpreted with caution. This phase Ib/II study was not designed or powered to directly compare combination therapy with tinengotinib monotherapy, and substantial differences in baseline characteristics, particularly prior exposure to ICIs and FGFR molecular profiles, limit cross-arm comparisons. Thus, we cannot exclude the possibility that the efficacy observed in Arm B was largely driven by tinengotinib alone. Notably, predefined exploratory subgroup analyses (Supplementary Table 8) suggest that the addition of atezolizumab may be associated with numerically improved efficacy compared with monotherapy. Nevertheless, these observations are based on small subgroup sizes and remain exploratory. Accordingly, the observed activity of the combination regimen should be viewed as hypothesis-generating, warranting further validation in larger, prospective studies specifically designed to assess the additional benefit of immunotherapy in this setting.

The safety profile is distinct from selective FGFR inhibitors, where hyperphosphatemia, due to FGFR1 inhibition, is the most frequently reported AE, often accompanied by alopecia, fatigue, nausea, dry mouth, and dry eye, all of which are related to quality of life32. In contrast, the most common grade ≥3 AEs observed with tinengotinib were hypertension and hematologic toxicities. Importantly, hypertension was generally manageable with standard antihypertensive therapy. Regarding other AEs, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia syndrome was also commonly observed, but grade ≥3 cases were rare. Despite its multi-targeted mechanism, tinengotinib demonstrated a favorable safety profile at the RP2D.

Tinengotinib also demonstrated preliminary activity in castration-resistant prostate cancer, where one patient achieved a confirmed CR. Furthermore, encouraging disease control was observed in patients with FGFR-altered advanced solid tumors, suggesting broader relevance of tinengotinib across FGFR-driven cancers. Tumor-agnostic strategies using FGFR inhibitors, such as erdafitinib, have recently shown promise across diverse tumor types harboring FGFR alterations33. In this context, prospective, biomarker-driven trials will be critical to defining the therapeutic role of tinengotinib across a wider oncologic spectrum.

This study has several limitations. First, this study is limited by its overall sample size and the small number of patients within specific molecular and clinical subgroups, which restricts the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding efficacy in defined populations. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and to better characterize treatment effects across distinct patient subsets. Second, the median follow-up duration remains insufficient for OS analysis, particularly in Arm B. Third, the study did not include mechanistic investigations to elucidate how tinengotinib overcomes FGFR inhibitor resistance and its synergistic mechanism when combined with ICI. An additional limitation is the absence of integrated translational analyses, such as post-treatment next-generation sequencing, which limits insight into resistance mechanisms and response biomarkers.

In conclusion, this phase Ib/II study suggests that tinengotinib, administered as monotherapy or in combination with atezolizumab, has a manageable safety profile and shows preliminary antitumor activity in patients with advanced solid tumors, particularly cholangiocarcinoma. Clinical activity signals were observed across several molecularly and clinically relevant subgroups, including patients with FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement, prior FGFR inhibitor exposure, or prior ICI treatment. The results support further clinical investigation of tinengotinib, both as monotherapy and in combination strategies, in larger, well-designed prospective trials.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: The study complied with all relevant ethical regulations and had been approved by the institutional review boards or independent ethics committees at each participating site (Ethics Committee of Peking University Cancer Hospital & Institute, Medical Ethics Committee of Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, Medical Ethics Committee of Shandong Cancer Hospital & Institute, Peking University Third Hospital Medical Science Research Ethics Committee, Jilin Province Cancer Hospital Institutional Review Board, Medical Ethics Review Committee of Hunan Cancer Hospital, Medical Ethics Committee of Henan Cancer Hospital, Institutional Review Board of Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital of Nanjing University Medical School). The study was authorized and the study design complied with all relevant regulations regarding the use of human subject participants and was conducted in accordance with the criteria set by the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.

This open-label, multicenter, phase Ⅰb/II trial enrolled participants into three predefined arms: Arm A (tinengotinib monotherapy in advanced solid tumors), Arm B (tinengotinib combined with atezolizumab in advanced BTC), and Arm C (tinengotinib combined with nab-paclitaxel in advanced triple negative breast cancer; terminated due to strategic reasons). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 4, each arm comprised a dose-escalation phase (phase Ⅰb) followed by a dose-expansion phase (phase II). The results reported in this paper pertain only to Arms A and B. Patients were enrolled between March 2022 and August 2024, and the data cutoff date for this analysis is August 31, 2024, which is also the study completion date. The study was pre-registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05253053) on Feb 23, 2022, and the complete protocol is available in the Supplementary Information.

Eligible participants were adults with locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors. For Arm A, tumor types included but were not limited to cholangiocarcinoma, small cell lung cancer, and HER2-negative breast cancer. Arm B enrolled patients with advanced, unresectable, non-ampullary BTC. Additional inclusion criteria for all arms included previously receiving standard therapies (unless contraindicated, not tolerated, or unavailable), and measurable or evaluable disease per RECIST 1.1. The study focused on sex, while no information on gender identity was collected or is available. Sex was not considered in the study design. Sex was determined based on self-reporting. FGFR alterations were measured by next-generation sequencing.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: In phase Ⅰb, a standard 3 + 3 dose-escalation design was employed to determine the dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and appropriate doses for expansion. The starting dose of tinengotinib was 8 mg orally once daily (QD). In Arm A, participants received tinengotinib monotherapy at 8 mg, 10 mg, or 12 mg QD, with each cycle defined as 21 consecutive days of treatment. In Arm B, tinengotinib was administered at the same dosing levels in combination with atezolizumab, which was given with 1200 mg intravenous infusions every 21 days.

sec.title: Endpoints and assessments
sec.p: The primary endpoints in both arms were safety, tolerability, identification of DLTs (defined as detailed in Supplementary Table 10), determination of the MTD, and dose selection for expansion. Secondary endpoints included preliminary efficacy and PK. In Arm A, efficacy outcomes included the best overall response (complete response [CR], partial response [PR], stable disease [SD], or progressive disease [PD]), ORR, disease control rate (DCR), DoR, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). In Arm B, the same endpoints were assessed.

Tumor assessments were conducted every 6 weeks. Measurable or evaluable disease at screening was defined according to RECIST version 1.1. In Arm A, tumor responses were evaluated using RECIST 1.1; for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, bone lesions were additionally assessed using PCWG3 criteria. In Arm B, which involved tinengotinib in combination with the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab, tumor responses were evaluated using both RECIST 1.1 and iRECIST to account for potential atypical response patterns associated with immunotherapy. Adverse events were graded per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. Survival status was collected every 3 months. For PK analysis, approximately 4 mL of blood was collected at designated timepoints as outlined in Supplementary Table 11.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The phase Ib dose-escalation part of Arms A and B followed a standard 3 + 3 design, with an anticipated enrollment of 9-18 participants. In the phase II expansion, each of Cohorts A1, A2, A3, and B planned to enroll approximately 20-30 participants.

The definitions of full-analysis set (FAS), safety analysis set (SAS), DLT analysis set, efficacy analysis set (EAS), and PK set were detailed in the protocol. ORR/iORR and DCR/iDCR were calculated with corresponding two-sided 95% CIs using the Clopper-Pearson method. Time-to-event endpoints were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Plasma concentration-time profiles were plotted, and noncompartmental analysis was performed using Phoenix WinNonlin software (version 8.3; Pharsight Corporation). All statistical analyses, excluding PK modeling, were conducted using SAS software (version 9.4; SAS Institute).
